front.title: Provider Authentication for More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI)

abstract.t: The MIMI protocol requires each provider to authenticate the provider that sends it a request. It specifies mutually authenticated TLS for this, but not where the client certificates come from or which trust anchors check them. The public Web PKI has stopped issuing such certificates. This document defines how MIMI providers authenticate each other without it. The mechanism every provider implements is a key published in DNS under the provider's domain, used to sign each request with HTTP Message Signatures. DANE client certificates, client certificates from configured PKIX trust anchors, and locally configured trust lists are defined as additional mechanisms that a provider can accept by local policy.

note.t: Status information for this document may be found at .

section.name: Introduction
section.t: In the MIMI protocol , providers send each other HTTPS requests: to fetch key material, to submit messages to a room's hub, and for the hub to fan messages out to the other providers in the room. Every one of those requests is acted on because of who sent it. A hub accepts a Commit because it came from a provider whose users are in the room. A follower accepts a notification because it came from the room's hub. If the source of a request is not authenticated, any host on the Internet can claim to be any provider.

Section 4.1 of says the TLS connection "MUST be mutually authenticated" and that the certificates "MUST authenticate the source and target provider domains". It does not say who issues the source provider's client certificate or which trust anchors the target uses to check it. explains why the answer cannot be "the public Web PKI". As a result, every deployment today either runs a private CA and asks each peer to install it, or does not authenticate peers at all. Neither is open federation, and neither interoperates without out-of-band setup that the protocol does not describe.
This document fills that gap. It defines:

list.t: A mandatory-to-implement mechanism (): the source provider publishes a public key in DNS under its own domain and signs each request with HTTP Message Signatures . TLS is server-authenticated only, using the provider's ordinary server certificate. This is the same trust model DKIM uses for email.

Three optional mechanisms: DANE client certificates (), PKIX client certificates checked against trust anchors the receiver configures (), and trust lists of keys or certificates configured per peer ().
Room for other mechanisms that providers agree on between themselves ().
How a receiver combines them by local policy (), and what it answers when authentication fails ().

section.t: proposes replacement text for Section 4.1 of .

section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document uses the terms "provider", "hub" and "follower" as defined in .

dd.t: The provider that sends a MIMI protocol request.
The domain name of the source provider, as named in the request's From header field (Section 4.1 of ).
The domain name that a mechanism in this document proves the request came from.

section.name: The Web PKI Has Left the Federation
section.t: The obvious source of a provider's client certificate used to be the public CA that issues its server certificate. For years those CAs added the id-kp-clientAuth extended key usage to server certificates as a matter of course, and servers presented them as client certificates to their peers. SMTP with mutual TLS, XMPP server-to-server federation, and a long list of HTTP APIs relied on this. It was never a promise. It was a side effect, and it has now been removed.

The Chrome Root Program decides which CAs Chrome trusts, and so, in practice, which CAs can sell a server certificate. Version 1.8 of its policy states the goal plainly: "to align all PKI hierarchies included in the Chrome Root Store on the principle of serving only TLS server authentication use cases". It then sets dates:

list.t: Subordinate CA certificates disclosed on or after 15 June 2026 may assert only id-kp-serverAuth.
Subscriber certificates issued on or after 15 March 2027 may assert only id-kp-serverAuth.
From 15 June 2026, hierarchies found in violation are phased out of Chrome, 90 days after the violation is detected. Multi-purpose roots are being removed from the store.

section.t: The enforcement is worth reading twice. Chrome does not forbid a CA from issuing client certificates. It only stops trusting the CA's server certificates if it does. Since server certificates are the CA's business, that is not a choice. Let's Encrypt removed the client-authentication EKU from its default profile on 11 February 2026 and retired its last profile offering it on 8 July 2026 . The other public CAs are following the same calendar.

None of this was aimed at MIMI, or at SMTP, or at XMPP. Those protocols were not consulted so much as noticed, the way a road crew notices whatever happens to be parked on the road. The policy is coherent from the point of view of a browser: a root store with exactly one purpose is easier to run, and every change to it now breaks only browsers. It is not a PKI that any other protocol should build on, and its operator has said so in writing.

So a MIMI provider cannot obtain a publicly trusted client certificate. What remains is a private CA, installed by hand at every peer, which turns an open federation into a set of bilateral agreements. This document takes the other road. A provider already proves control of its domain to get a server certificate, and a domain-validated certificate is issued on the strength of DNS. The provider can publish a key in that same DNS and leave the CA out of the client side entirely.

section.name: Overview
section.t: The source provider always sends its domain in the From header field (Section 4.1 of ). The target provider runs the mechanisms it accepts, in an order it chooses. A mechanism either produces an authenticated domain or fails. The request is authenticated if some mechanism's authenticated domain equals the source domain.

texttable.title: Provider authentication mechanisms
texttable.c: TLSA record, under the source domain

section.t: Every provider MUST implement both signing and verification for the DNS key mechanism. This is the only requirement that exists for interoperability: without one mechanism that every provider implements, two providers that each conform could have no mechanism in common. Implementing it does not oblige a provider to accept it. Which mechanisms a provider accepts, from which peers, is local policy ().
Responses are not signed. The source provider authenticates the target provider through the TLS server certificate, as with any HTTPS request.

section.name: DNS-Published Keys with HTTP Message Signatures
Key Records
section.t: A provider publishes each signing key as a DNS TXT record at the owner name:
The selector is a single DNS label chosen by the provider. It MUST NOT begin with an underscore. A provider MAY publish several keys under different selectors, for rotation or for separate servers.
The record data is a list of tag-value pairs. If the record consists of several character-strings, they are concatenated without separators before parsing, as in DKIM . The syntax, in ABNF :

figure.sourcecode: key-record = %s"v=MIMI1" *( *WSP ";" *WSP tag ) *WSP [";"] *WSP tag = tag-name *WSP "=" *WSP tag-value tag-name = ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" ) tag-value = *( %x21-3A / %x3C-7E ) ; any VCHAR except ";" WSP = SP / HTAB

section.t: The version tag v=MIMI1 MUST come first. A record that does not begin with it is not a MIMI key record and is ignored. This specification defines two further tags:

dd.t: The key type. This document defines ed25519, an Ed25519 public key . Verifiers MUST support ed25519. Other key types MAY be defined later.
The public key, in base64 with padding. For ed25519 it is the 32-byte public key. An empty value means the key under this selector has been revoked.

section.t: Verifiers MUST ignore tags they do not recognize, so that later specifications can add tags.
An example, using the Ed25519 test key from Appendix B.1.4 of :

section.name: Signing Requests
section.t: The source provider signs each MIMI protocol request with HTTP Message Signatures . The signature:

list.t: MUST cover the derived components @method and @target-uri, and the from header field. Covering from binds the signature to the source domain; without it, a valid signature from one provider could be attached to a request that claims to come from another.
MUST cover the content-digest field if the request has content. The Content-Digest field SHOULD use sha-256.
MUST include the created parameter and the keyid parameter, whose value is the selector of the key that made the signature.
SHOULD include the tag parameter with the value mimi, so that a verifier can find the MIMI signature on a request that carries others.
MAY cover other components and include other parameters, such as expires or nonce.

section.t: The signer MAY include the alg parameter. If present, it MUST match the key type in the key record (ed25519 for k=ed25519).
The @target-uri is the URL the source provider requests, taken from the target provider's directory (Section 5.1 of ).
shows a complete signed request.

section.name: Verifying Requests
section.t: To verify a request, the target provider:

list.t: Takes the source domain from the From header field.

Selects a signature from the Signature-Input field whose tag parameter is mimi, or, if there is none, any signature that covers the components listed in . A verifier MAY limit how many signatures it tries.
Checks that the signature covers the components required by and has created and keyid parameters.

Checks created. Verifiers SHOULD reject a signature created more than 300 seconds in the past or more than 60 seconds in the future. They MAY configure other limits. If expires is present and has passed, the signature MUST be rejected.
Queries TXT records at <keyid>._mimi.<source-domain>, and uses the first record that is a MIMI key record (). If there is none, or its p tag is empty, verification fails.
If the request has content, checks that Content-Digest matches it .
Verifies the signature over the signature base with the public key.

section.t: If all steps succeed, the authenticated domain is the source domain.

A verifier SHOULD use a DNSSEC-validating resolver when one is available. If validation of the key record's response is "bogus", verification fails. A verifier MAY, by local policy, require the response to be "secure".
A verifier MAY cache key records for their DNS TTL. It SHOULD NOT cache a negative or failed lookup for longer than the negative-caching TTL, so that a newly published key works promptly.

section.name: Key Rotation and Revocation
section.t: To rotate keys, a provider publishes the new key under a new selector, waits at least the TTL of the record, starts signing with the new selector, and then removes the old record. To revoke a key at once, it replaces the old record's p value with an empty value; this takes effect as caches expire. A short TTL on key records shortens both delays.

section.name: DANE Client Certificates
section.t: A provider that prefers TLS-layer authentication MAY present a client certificate that is authenticated by a DANE TLSA record, as specified in . It uses Format 1 of that specification, with the service label _mimi:

The TLSA record data and its matching rules are as in and . The source domain's zone MUST be DNSSEC-signed, and the target provider MUST treat the TLSA records as usable only if their validation status is "secure"; that is what DANE's security rests on.

The target provider requests a client certificate in the TLS handshake. It may not know the source domain until it reads the From header field of the first request. It then looks up the TLSA records for that domain and checks the client certificate against them. If they match, the authenticated domain is the source domain. The source provider MAY send the DANE Client Identity TLS extension defined in so that the target can fetch the records during the handshake.

section.name: PKIX Client Certificates from Configured Trust Anchors
section.t: Some providers operate where a PKIX hierarchy that still issues client certificates is required or already deployed: government PKIs, sector and enterprise PKIs, and federation operators that run a CA for their members. Such a provider MAY present a client certificate from that hierarchy, which is the mechanism Section 4.1 of describes today.
The certificate MUST contain a subjectAltName dNSName that is the provider domain. If it contains an extended key usage extension, that extension MUST include id-kp-clientAuth.

The target provider validates the certificate path per against trust anchors it configures for this purpose, applying whatever certificate policy constraints its deployment requires. It matches the provider domain against the certificate as a DNS-ID per ; it does not use the subject common name. If both succeed, the authenticated domain is the matched DNS name.

A target provider SHOULD NOT use a public Web PKI root store, such as the one its operating system or TLS library ships for server authentication, as the trust anchors for this mechanism. The CAs in those stores no longer issue client certificates (), and the ones that still might are the ones the store is about to drop.

section.name: Trust Lists
section.t: A target provider MAY configure, per peer domain, the keys or certificates it accepts from that peer:

list.t: An Ed25519 public key and its selector. Requests are verified as in , except that the key comes from configuration rather than DNS.
A certificate, a public key, or a CA certificate. The client certificate is checked against it at the TLS layer.

section.t: The authenticated domain is the peer domain the entry is configured for. This is how most deployments authenticate peers today, and it remains useful for private federations and testing. It requires out-of-band setup for every peer, so a provider that relies only on it cannot reach providers it has not been configured for.

section.name: Other Mechanisms
section.t: Providers MAY authenticate each other with other mechanisms that they have agreed on, whether bilaterally, within a federation, or by following another specification. This document does not describe such mechanisms and does not need to. A provider that accepts one treats it like any mechanism in this document: it produces an authenticated domain, and the rules in apply to it, including that the authenticated domain equal the source domain.
Using another mechanism with some peers does not change the requirement in to implement the DNS key mechanism, which is how a provider reaches peers it has agreed nothing with.

section.name: Local Policy
section.t: Each target provider decides which mechanisms it accepts, in which order, and whether the choice differs per peer. Some examples:

list.t: An open provider accepts DNS keys from anyone and the other mechanisms from peers that use them.
A provider in a regulated environment accepts only PKIX certificates under its sector's trust anchors, and DNS keys only with DNSSEC.
A private federation accepts only trust-listed peers.

section.t: A target provider MAY accept a request without authentication during a transition, for example to log which peers would fail before it starts refusing them. This is outside this specification, and such a provider gets none of the protection in .

Whatever mechanism is used, the authenticated domain MUST equal the source domain. This matters especially for the TLS-layer mechanisms: an HTTP connection authenticated with one provider's client certificate MUST NOT be used to authenticate a request whose From header field names another provider. Without this check, a provider with any valid credential could impersonate any other.

Authentication says only which provider sent the request. Whether that provider is allowed to make it, for example whether a notification really comes from the room's hub, is decided by and by the room's policy.

section.name: Errors
section.t: If no accepted mechanism authenticates the source domain, the target provider answers with status 403 (Forbidden) . It MAY include an Accept-Signature field (Section 5.1 of ) describing the signature it requires, and MAY include a problem details body saying why authentication failed.
Status 401 (Unauthorized) is not used, because requires a 401 response to carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge, and none of these mechanisms is an HTTP authentication scheme.
A target provider SHOULD NOT say in its response which mechanisms it tried or why each one failed beyond what the source provider needs to fix its configuration.

section.name: Replacement Text for the MIMI Protocol
section.t: This section proposes replacing the last paragraph of Section 4.1 of ("The TLS connection underlying the HTTPS connection MUST be mutually authenticated...") with:

li.t: The TLS connection underlying the HTTPS connection authenticates the target provider domain, according to . The target provider authenticates the source provider domain using one of the mechanisms in [this document]. Every provider implements the DNS key mechanism of [this document], Section 5; which mechanisms a provider accepts is local policy, and providers MAY use other mechanisms they have agreed on.

section.t: It also replaces the reference to , which obsoletes. The second sentence of the paragraph in Section 9 of that relies on "mutually-authenticated TLS" would change to refer to provider authentication generally.

section.name: DNS as the Root of Trust
section.t: Without DNSSEC, the DNS key mechanism is as strong as the target provider's view of DNS for the source domain. An attacker who can forge DNS responses to the target, or who controls the source domain's delegation, can substitute a key. This is the same exposure DKIM has. It is also the exposure domain-validated certificates have: a CA validates domain control through DNS or through HTTP to an address DNS gave it. An attacker who controls DNS for a domain can get a public server certificate for it. The DNS key mechanism removes the CA from the client side; it does not remove a protection that the Web PKI provided.
With DNSSEC, the key is authenticated by the zone's signature, and an off-path attacker cannot forge it. Deployments that need that assurance can require it () or use DANE ().

section.name: Replay
section.t: A signature is valid for any copy of the request within the created window. An attacker who records a signed request can replay it in that window, to the same target, provided the attacker can see the request at all; it is sent over TLS. Signers MAY include a nonce parameter and verifiers MAY track nonces for the window. Most MIMI requests are either idempotent or carry MLS messages that the hub will reject the second time, which limits the damage.

section.name: Key Compromise
section.t: A provider whose signing key is compromised revokes it as described in . Until caches expire, the attacker can sign requests as the provider. The record's TTL bounds that time.

section.name: Downgrade Between Mechanisms
section.t: An attacker cannot downgrade a target provider from a mechanism it requires to one it does not accept, since the target decides alone. A target that accepts several mechanisms is as strong as the weakest of them for any peer it accepts them from.

section.name: Same-Connection Impersonation
section.t: See the requirement in that the authenticated domain equal the source domain on every request, including requests on a connection whose client certificate was already accepted.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Key lookups tell the target provider's DNS resolver, and anyone who can observe its queries, which source providers the target provider hears from. This is the same information the source provider's TLS connection already reveals to a network observer, and it is about providers, not users. Caching reduces it.

front.title: Domain names - implementation and specification

abstract.t: This RFC is the revised specification of the protocol and format used in the implementation of the Domain Name System. It obsoletes RFC-883. This memo documents the details of the domain name client - server communication.

front.title: DNS Security Introduction and Requirements

abstract.t: The Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) add data origin authentication and data integrity to the Domain Name System. This document introduces these extensions and describes their capabilities and limitations. This document also discusses the services that the DNS security extensions do and do not provide. Last, this document describes the interrelationships between the documents that collectively describe DNSSEC. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF

abstract.t: Internet technical specifications often need to define a formal syntax. Over the years, a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications. The current specification documents ABNF. It balances compactness and simplicity with reasonable representational power. The differences between standard BNF and ABNF involve naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence, and value ranges. This specification also supplies additional rule definitions and encoding for a core lexical analyzer of the type common to several Internet specifications. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile

abstract.t: This memo profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and X.509 v2 certificate revocation list (CRL) for use in the Internet. An overview of this approach and model is provided as an introduction. The X.509 v3 certificate format is described in detail, with additional information regarding the format and semantics of Internet name forms. Standard certificate extensions are described and two Internet-specific extensions are defined. A set of required certificate extensions is specified. The X.509 v2 CRL format is described in detail along with standard and Internet-specific extensions. An algorithm for X.509 certification path validation is described. An ASN.1 module and examples are provided in the appendices. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: The DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol: TLSA

abstract.t: Encrypted communication on the Internet often uses Transport Layer Security (TLS), which depends on third parties to certify the keys used. This document improves on that situation by enabling the administrators of domain names to specify the keys used in that domain's TLS servers. This requires matching improvements in TLS client software, but no change in TLS server software. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: The DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) Protocol: Updates and Operational Guidance

abstract.t: This document clarifies and updates the DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) TLSA specification (RFC 6698), based on subsequent implementation experience. It also contains guidance for implementers, operators, and protocol developers who want to use DANE records.

front.title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)

abstract.t: This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA). The algorithm is instantiated with recommended parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves. An example implementation and test vectors are provided.

front.title: Scoped Interpretation of DNS Resource Records through "Underscored" Naming of Attribute Leaves

abstract.t: Formally, any DNS Resource Record (RR) may occur under any domain name. However, some services use an operational convention for defining specific interpretations of an RRset by locating the records in a DNS branch under the parent domain to which the RRset actually applies. The top of this subordinate branch is defined by a naming convention that uses a reserved node name, which begins with the underscore character (e.g., "_name"). The underscored naming construct defines a semantic scope for DNS record types that are associated with the parent domain above the underscored branch. This specification explores the nature of this DNS usage and defines the "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry with IANA. The purpose of this registry is to avoid collisions resulting from the use of the same underscored name for different services.

front.title: HTTP Semantics

abstract.t: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

front.title: HTTP Message Signatures

abstract.t: This document describes a mechanism for creating, encoding, and verifying digital signatures or message authentication codes over components of an HTTP message. This mechanism supports use cases where the full HTTP message may not be known to the signer and where the message may be transformed (e.g., by intermediaries) before reaching the verifier. This document also describes a means for requesting that a signature be applied to a subsequent HTTP message in an ongoing HTTP exchange.

front.title: Service Identity in TLS

abstract.t: Many application technologies enable secure communication between two entities by means of Transport Layer Security (TLS) with Internet Public Key Infrastructure using X.509 (PKIX) certificates. This document specifies procedures for representing and verifying the identity of application services in such interactions.
This document obsoletes RFC 6125.

front.title: Digest Fields

abstract.t: This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests. The Content-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP message content. The Repr-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP representations. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest can be used to indicate a sender's interest and preferences for receiving the respective Integrity fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest HTTP fields.

front.title: More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) using HTTPS and MLS

abstract.t: This document specifies the More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) transport protocol, which allows users of different messaging providers to interoperate in group chats (rooms), including to send and receive messages, share room policy, and add participants to and remove participants from rooms. MIMI describes messages between providers, leaving most aspects of the provider-internal client- server communication up to the provider. MIMI integrates the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol to provide end-to-end security assurances, including authentication of protocol participants, confidentiality of messages exchanged within a room, and agreement on the state of the room.

front.title: TLS Client Authentication via DANE TLSA records

abstract.t: The DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) protocol describes how to publish Transport Layer Security (TLS) server certificates or public keys in the DNS, using the TLSA resource record. This document describes how to use the TLSA record to publish client certificates or public keys, and also the rules and considerations for using them with TLS. In addition, it defines a new TLS extension, DANE Client Identity, to convey the client's domain name identity to the server.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Representation and Verification of Domain-Based Application Service Identity within Internet Public Key Infrastructure Using X.509 (PKIX) Certificates in the Context of Transport Layer Security (TLS)

abstract.t: Many application technologies enable secure communication between two entities by means of Internet Public Key Infrastructure Using X.509 (PKIX) certificates in the context of Transport Layer Security (TLS). This document specifies procedures for representing and verifying the identity of application services in such interactions. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Procedures for the Management of the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

abstract.t: This document defines the procedures that the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) uses when handling assignment and other requests related to the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number registry. It also discusses the rationale and principles behind these procedures and how they facilitate the long-term sustainability of the registry.

This document updates IANA's procedures by obsoleting the previous UDP and TCP port assignment procedures defined in Sections 8 and 9.1 of the IANA Allocation Guidelines, and it updates the IANA service name and port assignment procedures for UDP-Lite, the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP), and the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP). It also updates the DNS SRV specification to clarify what a service name is and how it is registered. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

front.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures

abstract.t: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) permits a person, role, or organization that owns the signing domain to claim some responsibility for a message by associating the domain with the message. This can be an author's organization, an operational relay, or one of their agents. DKIM separates the question of the identity of the Signer of the message from the purported author of the message. Assertion of responsibility is validated through a cryptographic signature and by querying the Signer's domain directly to retrieve the appropriate public key. Message transit from author to recipient is through relays that typically make no substantive change to the message content and thus preserve the DKIM signature.
This memo obsoletes RFC 4871 and RFC 5672. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

front.title: Handling Long Lines in Content of Internet-Drafts and RFCs

abstract.t: This document defines two strategies for handling long lines in width-bounded text content. One strategy, called the "single backslash" strategy, is based on the historical use of a single backslash ('\') character to indicate where line-folding has occurred, with the continuation occurring with the first character that is not a space character (' ') on the next line. The second strategy, called the "double backslash" strategy, extends the first strategy by adding a second backslash character to identify where the continuation begins and is thereby able to handle cases not supported by the first strategy. Both strategies use a self-describing header enabling automated reconstitution of the original content.

front.title: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

abstract.t: This document defines a "problem detail" to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs.
This document obsoletes RFC 7807.

section.t: The target provider b.example reads a.example from From, looks up s1._mimi.a.example, and verifies the Ed25519 signature over this base. Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so an implementation can check its signer against these bytes.

list.t: Section 4.1 of has an editor's note asking whether From is the right field for the source domain. If the WG replaces it, the signature covers the new field instead.
The directory document could advertise which mechanisms a provider accepts, so a source provider knows before its first request. This document does not define that.

Keys could also be published in the directory document instead of DNS. That would rest their trust on the target's TLS server certificate, which is to say on the Web PKI, which is the thing this document is trying to stop depending on for the client side.
Whether nonces should be required rather than optional.

This section records the status of known implementations of the protocol defined by this specification at the time of posting of this Internet-Draft, and is based on a proposal described in . The description of implementations in this section is intended to assist the IETF in its decision processes in progressing drafts to RFCs. Please note that the listing of any individual implementation here does not imply endorsement by the IETF. Furthermore, no effort has been spent to verify the information presented here that was supplied by IETF contributors. This is not intended as, and must not be construed to be, a catalog of available implementations or their features. Readers are advised to note that other implementations may exist.

According to , "this will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature. It is up to the individual working groups to use this information as they see fit".

mimid (Review Commit, LLC): an open-source MIMI provider. It implements RFC 9421 signing and verification with the profile in , with keys from trust lists (). The DNS key mechanism, PKIX and DANE client certificates are being implemented. It signs every outbound request and can either refuse or log unauthenticated inbound requests.
